finding.claim: DELETE /reports/:id calls the async authorize() without await, so the delete at line 21 runs before the grant check result is known. Any user can delete reports they lack delete grants on, and a failed grant check becomes an unhandled rejection that can crash the process.
finding.source: DELETE /reports/:id route, req.params.id (server.js:19) and req.user from req.session.user (server.js:5)

trace.note: authorize(...) called without await; returns a promise that is discarded
remove executes before grant result is checked
If grants lack 'delete', authorize throws 403 into a discarded promise, which is unhandled

finding.guards_checked: authorize() grant check (server.js:9-16) is correct but its result is not awaited or used on the DELETE route; PUT route (server.js:27) awaits its check correctly, so the defect is specific to DELETE. Session middleware is not in the repo, so the unauthenticated case is unverified.

verdict.guard_found: None effective. The authorize() grant check at server.js:9-16 is a bare, un-awaited call at server.js:20 (`authorize(req.user, "delete", report);`), so its returned promise is discarded and its 403 throw becomes an unhandled rejection. Nothing between the request and db.reports.remove at server.js:21 checks the result. The PUT route at server.js:27 uses `await authorize(...)` and is not affected.
verdict.reason: The trace matches the code: server.js:20 calls authorize() without await, so execution reaches the remove at server.js:21 while the grant check at server.js:10-14 is still pending and its 403 is discarded, so any authenticated user (req.user from the session at server.js:5) can delete reports they hold no delete grant for. The unauthenticated case depends on session middleware that is not in the repo, but the authenticated low-privilege case is enough to confirm.
